record.original_question: Does every regular tournament, meaning an orientation of a complete graph in which each vertex has the same in-degree and out-degree, have its arc set decomposable into Hamilton cycles?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.1 (Kelly 196?). The arc set of every regular tournament can be decomposed into Hamilton cycles.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A tournament is an orientation of a complete graph; equivalently, a directed graph on a finite vertex set in which, for every pair of distinct vertices u and v, exactly one of the arcs (u,v) or (v,u) is present. A tournament is regular if every vertex has the same in-degree and the same out-degree (necessarily (n−1)/2 each, so n is odd). A Hamilton cycle in a directed graph is a directed cycle that visits every vertex exactly once. A decomposition of the arc set into Hamilton cycles is a partition of the arc set into subsets, each of which forms the arc set of a Hamilton cycle.

Prove or disprove: for every regular tournament T, the arc set of T can be partitioned into Hamilton cycles.
artifact.status_search_result: Kelly's conjecture was proved by Kühn and Osthus for all sufficiently large regular tournaments (Advances in Mathematics, 2013), as a special case of their result on Hamilton decompositions of robustly expanding regular digraphs. The conjecture in full generality (for all n) is not known to have been verified for small cases beyond what follows from the Kühn–Osthus threshold, so the conjecture is considered solved for large n / partially solved overall.

status_evidence.title: Hamilton decompositions of regular expanders: a proof of Kelly's conjecture for large tournaments
status_evidence.snippet: Kühn and Osthus prove Kelly's conjecture for large tournaments via robust expansion.
status_evidence.claim: Kelly's conjecture is proved for all sufficiently large regular tournaments.

status_evidence.title: A proof of Kelly's conjecture for large tournaments (Osthus talk)
status_evidence.snippet: Talk slides describing the proof of Kelly's conjecture for large n.
status_evidence.claim: Result holds for n sufficiently large, leaving small cases unaddressed by this method.
